n: The prophetic community under Elisha is growing, and their meeting place has become too small.
They propose going to the Jordan, where trees grow along the banks, to cut beams and build a larger place. Elisha agrees.
One asks Elisha to come with them, and he does. They value his presence even in ordinary work.
At the Jordan they begin cutting timber.
An iron axe head flies off into the river. The man is distressed because it was borrowed; iron tools were costly, and a poor man might have to work off the debt.
Elisha throws a stick where it sank, and the iron floats to the surface. The Lord cares about small, practical worries as well as great crises.
Elisha has the man pick it up himself.
Aram’s king plans ambushes along Israel’s border, choosing secret campsites.
Elisha warns Israel’s king to avoid each place where the Arameans are waiting.
The king heeds the warnings and is saved again and again.
Aram’s king is furious, convinced there is a traitor among his officers.
An officer explains: no traitor—Elisha the prophet knows even what the king says in his bedroom. Nothing is hidden from God.

f.w: the words that thou speakest in thy bedchamber

n: The king sends spies and learns that Elisha is at Dothan, a town north of Samaria.

f.g: a town where Joseph was once sold by his brothers.

n: An army with horses and chariots surrounds Dothan by night—an absurd show of force against one prophet.
Elisha’s servant goes out at dawn, sees the army, and panics.
Elisha calmly says, “Don’t be afraid—those with us outnumber those with them.” This is one of scripture’s great statements of faith.

f.w: they that be with us are more than they that be with them

n: Elisha prays for his servant’s eyes to be opened. The young man then sees the hills filled with fiery horses and chariots surrounding Elisha. The unseen hosts of heaven are real.
As the soldiers approach, Elisha prays that they be struck with blindness—probably a confusion or inability to recognize what they saw.

f.g: Hebrew sanwerim: a dazzling or bewildering blindness, also used in Genesis 19:11.

n: Elisha tells them, truthfully in a sense, that this isn’t the right place, and leads them about ten miles to Samaria—into the heart of Israel’s capital.
Inside Samaria, Elisha prays again, and their eyes are opened. They find themselves trapped in the enemy’s capital.
Israel’s king eagerly asks, “My father, shall I kill them?”

f.g: a title of respect for a prophet.

n: Elisha says no—feed them and send them home. Kindness to an enemy is a striking choice that anticipates the Savior’s teaching to love one’s enemies.

f.w: set bread and water before them

n: The king throws a great feast and sends them home. The Aramean raiding parties stop coming—mercy accomplished what force could not.
Later—perhaps years later—Ben-hadad launches a full-scale invasion and besieges Samaria.

The siege causes terrible famine. A donkey’s head—unclean and nearly inedible—sells for eighty silver pieces, and a small measure of dove’s dung (perhaps a nickname for a poor-quality bean or seed pod) for five.

f.g: possibly literal, used as fuel, or a popular name for wild seed pods.

n: As the king walks along the city wall, a woman cries out for help.
The king replies bitterly: if the Lord doesn’t help you, how can I? There is no grain on the threshing floor or wine in the press.

f.g: threshing floor, where grain was processed.
where grapes were crushed for wine.

n: She tells a horrifying story: two mothers agreed to eat their sons, one each day. The law had warned that such horrors would come if Israel broke the covenant.

f.w: Give thy son, that we may eat him

n: After they ate her son, the other woman hid hers. The siege has broken all human decency.
The king tears his robe, revealing he has been wearing sackcloth underneath—outward signs of mourning, though not necessarily true repentance.

f.g: rough cloth worn in grief or penitence.

n: Rather than turning to God, the king blames Elisha and vows to behead him that very day—perhaps because Elisha had counseled holding out.

f.w: God do so and more also to me
f.g: an oath: ‘May God punish me severely if I fail.’

n: Elisha, at home with the city’s elders, knows an executioner is coming and calls the king “this son of a murderer”—Ahab’s son, heir to Naboth’s murder. He tells them to hold the door, for the king himself is close behind.

The messenger (or the king himself) arrives, saying, “This disaster is from the Lord—why should I wait for Him any longer?” It is a cry of despair. The answer to that question comes in the next chapter.

f.w: what should I wait for the LORD any longer?
